items._section: Clause 5 - PIMS-specific requirements related to ISO/IEC 27001 (extends ISMS clauses 4-10 to privacy)

items.Title: Organizational controls - privacy guidance
items.Requirement / guidance: Apply privacy-specific guidance to organizational controls (e.g. policies, asset inventory to include PII inventory, classification of PII, supplier/third-party PII processing terms, incident management covering PII breaches).
items.Why CIA is involved: Extends organizational security controls specifically to protect the confidentiality of PII.
items.Evidence to verify: PII asset/data inventory, supplier PII clauses, PII breach procedure
items._section: Clause 6 - PIMS-specific guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002 controls (privacy overlay on the 93 security controls)

items.Title: People controls - privacy guidance
items.Requirement / guidance: Apply privacy-specific guidance to people controls (e.g. screening, terms of employment, awareness/training on PII handling, confidentiality obligations).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 6 - PIMS-specific guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002 controls (privacy overlay on the 93 security controls)

items.Title: Physical controls - privacy guidance
items.Requirement / guidance: Apply privacy-specific guidance to physical controls (e.g. secure areas/media handling where PII is stored or processed physically).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Physical control review for locations holding PII
items._section: Clause 6 - PIMS-specific guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002 controls (privacy overlay on the 93 security controls)

items.Title: Technological controls - privacy guidance
items.Requirement / guidance: Apply privacy-specific guidance to technological controls (e.g. access control, cryptography, data masking/de-identification, deletion, logging) specifically for systems processing PII.
items.Why CIA is involved: Technical controls (encryption, masking, access control, deletion) directly protect confidentiality and integrity of PII.
items.Evidence to verify: Technical control mapping to PII systems (encryption, masking, deletion)
items._section: Clause 6 - PIMS-specific guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002 controls (privacy overlay on the 93 security controls)

items.Title: Conditions for collection and processing
items.Requirement / guidance: Identify and document the lawful basis for processing, ensure PII is collected/processed only for identified, specific, explicit and legitimate purposes; determine and comply with obligations to PII principals; obtain/record consent where relied upon; conduct privacy impact assessments where required.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Legal basis register, consent records, PIA/DPIA reports
items._section: Clause 7 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII controllers

items.Title: Obligations to PII principals
items.Requirement / guidance: Provide transparent information to PII principals; support their rights (access, correction, erasure, objection); establish mechanisms for requests and complaints; handle automated decision-making per policy.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy notices, data-subject rights procedure and request log
items._section: Clause 7 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII controllers

items.Title: Privacy by design and privacy by default
items.Requirement / guidance: Limit collection/processing to what is adequate, relevant and limited to purpose (minimisation); de-identify/delete PII when no longer needed; ensure PII disposal at end of retention; design temporary files and system-generated data to protect privacy.
items.Why CIA is involved: Minimisation, de-identification and deletion directly reduce confidentiality exposure of PII.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy-by-design records, retention/deletion schedule, temp-file handling policy
items._section: Clause 7 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII controllers

items.Title: PII sharing, transfer and disclosure
items.Requirement / guidance: Identify the basis for transfers between jurisdictions/organizations; document and communicate applicable transfer mechanisms; record and manage disclosures to third parties, incl. legally mandated disclosures.
items.Why CIA is involved: Controls over sharing/transfer/disclosure directly govern who may access PII and under what safeguards.
items.Evidence to verify: Transfer/disclosure register, cross-border transfer mechanism records (e.g. SCCs)
items._section: Clause 7 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII controllers

items.Title: Conditions for collection and processing
items.Requirement / guidance: Process PII only per documented instructions of the controller (incl. for transfers); ensure the contract with the controller addresses PII processing; assist the controller in fulfilling its obligations.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: Obligations to PII principals
items.Requirement / guidance: Assist the controller in providing information to and fulfilling the rights of PII principals, per contract; do not respond directly to PII principals unless authorized.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Processor support procedure for data-subject rights requests
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: Privacy by design and privacy by default
items.Requirement / guidance: Apply temporary files/data minimisation, retention/return/disposal of PII at contract end or on instruction, and ensure sub-processing arrangements uphold the same privacy protections.
items.Why CIA is involved: Return/disposal at contract end and sub-processor flow-down protect confidentiality of PII across the processing chain.
items.Evidence to verify: Sub-processor register and flow-down clauses, end-of-contract deletion/return evidence
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: PII sharing, transfer and disclosure
items.Requirement / guidance: Notify the controller of legally binding requests for disclosure, of any unauthorized access/breach, and of the use of sub-processors; disclose/transfer PII only per controller instructions and applicable transfer mechanisms.
items.Why CIA is involved: Breach notification and controlled disclosure protect confidentiality and preserve accountable, unaltered handling of PII.
items.Evidence to verify: Sub-processor notifications, breach notification to controller, disclosure records
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: PIMS-specific reference controls for PII controllers
items.Requirement / guidance: Implement the Annex A control set (mapped to the Clause 7 categories above: conditions for collection/processing, obligations to PII principals, privacy by design/default, sharing/transfer/disclosure) as the certifiable controller control objectives, selected via the PIMS risk assessment and SoA.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Controller SoA with Annex A controls selected/justified
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: PIMS-specific reference controls for PII processors
items.Requirement / guidance: Implement the Annex B control set (mapped to the Clause 8 categories above) as the certifiable processor control objectives, selected via the PIMS risk assessment and SoA.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Processor SoA with Annex B controls selected/justified
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: Mapping annexes (ISO/IEC 29100, GDPR, ISO/IEC 27018 and 29151)
items.Requirement / guidance: Use the informative mapping annexes to cross-reference PIMS controls to the ISO/IEC 29100 privacy framework, GDPR articles, and cloud-PII-specific standards ISO/IEC 27018 and 29151.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - privacy governance/rights-based requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Cross-reference table used for GDPR/29100 alignment (see Tab 9 GDPR)
items._section: Clause 8 - Additional ISO/IEC 27002 guidance for PII processors

items.Title: Anticipate and prevent privacy-invasive events before they happen
items.Design practice: Identify privacy risks at the concept/planning stage of any new product, feature, AI system or process - before design begins - rather than reacting after a breach or complaint.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy risk register maintained from project inception; pre-project privacy screening checklist
items._section: Principle 1 - Proactive not Reactive; Preventative not Remedial

items.Title: Make privacy a stated organizational commitment
items.Design practice: Adopt a documented commitment (policy/charter) that privacy protection is a default objective of every product and process, with leadership accountability.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Principle 1 - Proactive not Reactive; Preventative not Remedial

items.Title: Learn from past incidents to prevent recurrence
items.Design practice: Use lessons from privacy incidents/near-misses (internal or industry-wide) to strengthen design standards and checklists proactively.
items.Why CIA is involved: Feeding incident lessons back into design standards preserves the integrity of the privacy-engineering process over time.
items._section: Principle 1 - Proactive not Reactive; Preventative not Remedial

items.Title: Collect and retain only what is necessary by default
items.Design practice: Ensure default settings require no action by the individual to protect their privacy: minimal data collection, shortest necessary retention, and narrowest default sharing.
items.Why CIA is involved: Default minimisation directly reduces the volume of data exposed to confidentiality risk.
items.Evidence to verify: Default configuration review, data minimisation and retention schedule
items._section: Principle 2 - Privacy as the Default Setting

items.Title: Purpose limitation is enforced by default
items.Design practice: Configure systems so data collected for one purpose is not automatically available for a different, incompatible purpose without a fresh assessment.
items.Why CIA is involved: Restricting purpose-based access is an access-control mechanism protecting confidentiality.
items.Evidence to verify: Purpose-limitation controls in data architecture (tagging, access scoping)
items._section: Principle 2 - Privacy as the Default Setting

items.Title: Opt-in, not opt-out, for anything beyond the necessary minimum
items.Design practice: Any processing beyond what is strictly necessary (e.g. marketing, analytics, AI training on user data) requires an affirmative, informed choice rather than being pre-enabled.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Principle 2 - Privacy as the Default Setting

items.Title: Treat privacy as a core design requirement, not an add-on
items.Design practice: Include privacy requirements in the same requirements/specification documents as functional and security requirements, from the first design iteration.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Design requirements documents with an explicit privacy-requirements section
items._section: Principle 3 - Privacy Embedded into Design

items.Title: Conduct a privacy/data protection impact assessment for the design
items.Design practice: Perform a DPIA/PIA (or AI system impact assessment for AI features) as part of the design process for any processing likely to pose meaningful privacy risk, and feed findings back into the design.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: DPIA/AISIA reports linked to design decisions
items._section: Principle 3 - Privacy Embedded into Design

items.Title: Apply privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) where they fit the design
items.Design practice: Evaluate and apply techniques such as pseudonymisation, anonymisation, differential privacy, encryption, or federated/on-device learning where they can reduce privacy risk without breaking functionality.
items.Why CIA is involved: PETs such as pseudonymisation, anonymisation and encryption directly reduce confidentiality exposure and can also preserve data integrity guarantees during processing.
items.Evidence to verify: PET evaluation and adoption records per system
items._section: Principle 3 - Privacy Embedded into Design

items.Title: Avoid false trade-offs between privacy and functionality/security
items.Design practice: Seek design solutions that achieve both the business/functional goal and strong privacy protection, rather than accepting privacy as the item traded away under time or cost pressure.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Design trade-off record showing privacy considered alongside functionality/security, not sacrificed by default
items._section: Principle 4 - Full Functionality - Positive-Sum, not Zero-Sum

items.Title: Demonstrate that privacy and security reinforce each other
items.Design practice: Show, for security-relevant features, how the chosen design serves both security and privacy objectives together (e.g. access control that both secures data and limits who can see personal data).
items.Why CIA is involved: Well-designed access, encryption and monitoring controls simultaneously protect confidentiality, integrity and availability while also serving privacy goals - the two are not in tension.
items.Evidence to verify: Combined privacy/security design rationale for key features
items._section: Principle 4 - Full Functionality - Positive-Sum, not Zero-Sum

items.Title: Protect personal data from collection to secure destruction
items.Design practice: Apply appropriate security controls (access control, encryption, monitoring) across the entire data lifecycle: collection, transmission, storage, use, sharing, archiving, and secure deletion/destruction.
items.Why CIA is involved: This principle is explicitly about applying full-lifecycle security - confidentiality, integrity and availability - to personal data.
items.Evidence to verify: Lifecycle data-flow diagram with security controls mapped to each stage
items._section: Principle 5 - End-to-End Security - Full Lifecycle Protection

items.Title: Ensure secure retention and disposal
items.Design practice: Define and enforce retention periods per data category, and ensure secure, verifiable destruction or anonymisation of personal data once no longer needed.
items.Why CIA is involved: Timely, verifiable deletion reduces confidentiality exposure from data retained beyond its need.
items._section: Principle 5 - End-to-End Security - Full Lifecycle Protection

items.Title: Extend security requirements to third parties in the data chain
items.Design practice: Ensure any processor, sub-processor or partner handling the personal data as part of the design maintains equivalent end-to-end security.
items.Why CIA is involved: Security must follow the data wherever it flows, including to third parties, to maintain confidentiality, integrity and availability throughout the chain.
items.Evidence to verify: Third-party security requirements in contracts, verification/audit evidence
items._section: Principle 5 - End-to-End Security - Full Lifecycle Protection

items.Title: Design components and operations to be independently verifiable
items.Design practice: Build the system so its privacy practices can be independently verified (e.g. via audit logs, documentation, or third-party assessment), not just asserted in a policy.
items.Why CIA is involved: Verifiable, tamper-resistant records of what the system actually does with data support the integrity of transparency claims.
items.Evidence to verify: Auditable design documentation, independent assessment/certification where applicable
items._section: Principle 6 - Visibility and Transparency

items.Title: Make privacy practices visible to users and stakeholders
items.Design practice: Ensure privacy notices, settings and data flows are clear, accessible and accurately reflect what the design actually does - avoid gaps between stated policy and actual behaviour.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy notice accuracy review against actual system behaviour
items._section: Principle 6 - Visibility and Transparency

items.Title: Provide accountability mechanisms for complaints and redress
items.Design practice: Design in a clear channel for individuals to raise privacy concerns about the specific product/feature, with a defined response process.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Complaint/redress channel and handling procedure for the design
items._section: Principle 6 - Visibility and Transparency

items.Title: Design around the interests of the individual, not just the organization
items.Design practice: Make user-centric choices the default in the design: strong privacy defaults, clear consent flows, and easy-to-find control over one's own data.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: User-centric design review, usability testing on privacy controls
items._section: Principle 7 - Respect for User Privacy - Keep it User-Centric

items.Title: Give individuals meaningful control over their own data
items.Design practice: Provide accessible mechanisms within the design for individuals to access, correct, export or delete their data and withdraw consent, without undue friction.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Self-service privacy controls (access, correction, deletion, export, consent withdrawal) built into the product
items._section: Principle 7 - Respect for User Privacy - Keep it User-Centric

items.Title: Communicate in clear, understandable language
items.Design practice: Ensure privacy-related information presented within the design (notices, prompts, settings) is written in plain, non-technical, non-legalistic language appropriate to the audience.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - user-centric/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Plain-language review of in-product privacy communications
items._section: Principle 7 - Respect for User Privacy - Keep it User-Centric

items.Title: Designing capabilities to enable consumers to enforce their privacy rights
items.Requirement: Design the product/service so consumers can exercise their privacy rights (e.g. access, correction, deletion, withdrawal of consent) directly through the product, not only through an external process.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: In-product rights-enforcement mechanisms, UX flow for exercising rights
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Developing capability to determine consumer privacy preferences
items.Requirement: Provide a means for consumers to set, view and change their privacy preferences, and ensure the product respects those preferences throughout use.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Designing human computer interface (HCI) for privacy
items.Requirement: Design the user interface so privacy information and controls are discoverable, understandable and usable, avoiding dark patterns that discourage privacy-protective choices.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: HCI/UX design review for privacy controls, dark-pattern audit
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Assigning relevant roles and authorities
items.Requirement: Assign clear roles and decision-making authority for privacy-by-design activities across the organization (e.g. product, engineering, legal, security).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Establishing multi-functional responsibilities
items.Requirement: Ensure privacy responsibilities are coordinated across the multiple functions involved in a consumer product's lifecycle (design, engineering, marketing, support, security).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Developing privacy knowledge, skill and ability
items.Requirement: Build the privacy knowledge, skills and abilities of staff involved in designing, building and operating the consumer product.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy-by-design training curriculum and completion records
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Ensuring knowledge of privacy controls
items.Requirement: Ensure relevant staff understand the specific privacy controls built into the product and how to operate/maintain them correctly.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Control-specific operational guidance and staff sign-off
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Documentation and information management
items.Requirement: Establish documentation and information-management practices covering the product's privacy design, decisions and controls, kept current and accessible to those who need it.
items.Why CIA is involved: Documentation integrity ensures design decisions and control records remain an accurate, unaltered basis for later audits and changes.
items._section: Clause 4 - General - organizational foundations for privacy by design

items.Title: Provision of privacy information
items.Requirement: Provide consumers with clear, accurate, accessible privacy information about the product (what is collected, why, how used, retained and shared).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 5 - Consumer communication requirements

items.Title: Accountability for providing privacy information
items.Requirement: Assign clear accountability within the organization for ensuring privacy information given to consumers is accurate, current and properly delivered.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Accountable owner for consumer privacy communications
items._section: Clause 5 - Consumer communication requirements

items.Title: Responding to consumer inquiries and complaints
items.Requirement: Establish a process to receive, track and respond to consumer privacy inquiries and complaints about the product in a timely manner.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Consumer privacy inquiry/complaint log and response-time tracking
items._section: Clause 5 - Consumer communication requirements

items.Title: Communicating to diverse consumer population
items.Requirement: Ensure privacy communications are accessible and understandable across the diversity of the consumer population (language, literacy, disability, age, context of use).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Accessibility/plain-language review of privacy communications across user segments
items._section: Clause 5 - Consumer communication requirements

items.Title: Prepare data breach communications
items.Requirement: Prepare, in advance, communication plans and templates for notifying consumers in the event of a data breach affecting the product.
items.Why CIA is involved: Breach communications are triggered by loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability of consumer data and must accurately convey that impact.
items.Evidence to verify: Pre-drafted consumer breach-notification templates and trigger criteria
items._section: Clause 5 - Consumer communication requirements

items.Title: Conducting a privacy risk assessment
items.Requirement: Conduct a privacy risk assessment for the consumer product considering the consumer's perspective, context and reasonably foreseeable uses/misuses.
items.Why CIA is involved: Privacy risk assessment centers on the risk of unauthorized exposure or misuse of consumer data - a confidentiality risk.
items._section: Clause 6 - Risk management requirements

items.Title: Assessing privacy capabilities of third parties
items.Requirement: Assess the privacy capabilities of third parties (suppliers, component providers, service partners) involved in the product's data processing.
items.Why CIA is involved: Ensures third parties handling consumer data maintain adequate confidentiality safeguards.
items.Evidence to verify: Third-party privacy capability assessment/due diligence records
items._section: Clause 6 - Risk management requirements

items.Title: Establishing and documenting requirements for privacy controls
items.Requirement: Based on the risk assessment, establish and document the specific privacy control requirements the product must meet.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Clause 6 - Risk management requirements

items.Title: Monitoring and updating risk assessment
items.Requirement: Monitor the product and its context for change and update the privacy risk assessment periodically or when significant changes occur.
items.Why CIA is involved: Ongoing monitoring for new confidentiality/exposure risk as the product or its data uses change.
items.Evidence to verify: Risk assessment review schedule and update records
items._section: Clause 6 - Risk management requirements

items.Title: Including privacy risks in cybersecurity resilience design
items.Requirement: Ensure privacy risks are explicitly considered as part of the product's cybersecurity resilience design, so privacy and security risk treatment are integrated rather than siloed.
items.Why CIA is involved: This requirement explicitly ties privacy risk into cybersecurity resilience design, spanning confidentiality, integrity and availability.
items._section: Clause 6 - Risk management requirements

items.Title: Integrating design/operation of privacy controls into product development and management lifecycles
items.Requirement: Embed privacy-control design and operation activities into the standard product development and management lifecycle (e.g. stage gates, sprints, release processes), not as a separate parallel track.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy checkpoints embedded in the product development lifecycle
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Designing privacy controls
items.Requirement: Design specific privacy controls (technical and procedural) that meet the documented requirements from 6.4, appropriate to the product and its risks.
items.Why CIA is involved: Designed controls exist specifically to protect the confidentiality of consumer data collected/processed by the product.
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Implementing privacy controls
items.Requirement: Implement the designed privacy controls in the product as built, ensuring the as-built product matches the as-designed privacy controls.
items.Why CIA is involved: Implementation must faithfully deliver the confidentiality protections the design specified.
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Designing privacy control testing
items.Requirement: Design and perform testing of privacy controls to verify they function as intended before and after release.
items.Why CIA is involved: Testing verifies both that data stays protected (confidentiality) and that controls function correctly and consistently (integrity).
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy control test plans and results
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Managing the transition of privacy controls
items.Requirement: Manage changes to privacy controls over time (updates, replacements, migrations) so protection is maintained through transitions.
items.Why CIA is involved: Transitions must preserve the integrity of privacy protection - no gap or regression introduced by the change.
items.Evidence to verify: Change management records for privacy controls
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Managing the operation of privacy controls
items.Requirement: Operate privacy controls on an ongoing basis once deployed, including monitoring that they continue to function as intended.
items.Why CIA is involved: Ongoing operation must maintain confidentiality, integrity and availability of the privacy protections throughout the product's active life.
items.Evidence to verify: Operational monitoring of privacy controls in production
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Preparing for and managing a privacy breach
items.Requirement: Prepare an incident response capability specific to privacy breaches affecting the product, and manage actual breaches through detection, containment, assessment and remediation.
items.Why CIA is involved: Privacy breaches are, by definition, failures of confidentiality, integrity or availability that must be detected and remediated.
items.Evidence to verify: Privacy breach response plan and incident records
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Operating privacy controls for dependent processes/products throughout the PII lifecycle
items.Requirement: Ensure privacy controls also operate correctly across the processes and third-party products/services the in-scope product depends on, throughout the PII lifecycle.
items.Why CIA is involved: Protection must extend across the full chain of dependent processes/products handling the PII, covering confidentiality, integrity and availability throughout.
items.Evidence to verify: Dependency mapping with privacy-control coverage confirmed end-to-end
items._section: Clause 7 - Developing, deploying and operating designed privacy controls

items.Title: Designing privacy controls for retirement and end of use
items.Requirement: Design privacy controls for the product's retirement/end-of-use stage: secure deletion or return of consumer PII, and winding down of data processing when the product is discontinued or the consumer stops using it.
items.Why CIA is involved: Secure deletion/return at end of use prevents unauthorized retention or exposure of consumer data after the product's active life.
items.Evidence to verify: Retirement/end-of-use data deletion or return procedure and verification
items._section: Clause 8 - End of PII lifecycle requirements

items.Title: Illustrative use cases and analysis
items.Requirement: A Technical Report (not a certifiable requirements document) providing worked, illustrative use cases and analysis to help engineers and practitioners interpret and apply the Part 1 requirements above to real consumer-product scenarios.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - consumer-facing UX/organizational design practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Use Part 2's worked examples as a reference when interpreting ambiguous Part 1 requirements for your own product context
items._section: Part 2 - ISO/IEC TR 31700-2:2023 - Use cases (informative companion to Part 1)

items.Title: Scope
items.Requirement: Determine applicability: DORA applies to a broad list of EU financial entities (credit institutions, payment/e-money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers, CCPs/CSDs/trading venues, insurers, pension institutions, credit rating agencies, crowdfunding providers, etc.), with limited exclusions for certain small entities.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Chapter I - General provisions

items.Title: Proportionality
items.Requirement: Apply DORA requirements proportionate to size, risk profile, and nature/scale/complexity of services; smaller/less-complex entities may use the simplified framework (Art.16).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Chapter I - General provisions

items.Title: Governance and organisation
items.Requirement: The management body bears ultimate responsibility for ICT risk: defines risk appetite, approves ICT security policies and the ICT risk management framework, approves ICT budget/staffing/training, approves major ICT projects, ensures a crisis communication plan and internal audit of ICT risk; at least one board member reports on ICT risk.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Board-approved ICT risk appetite, policies, budget and project approvals; board reporting line on ICT risk
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: ICT risk management framework
items.Requirement: Maintain a robust, well-documented ICT risk management framework (strategies, policies, procedures, protocols, tools) that minimises the impact of ICT risk; document and review the function periodically, after major incidents, and at least annually.
items.Why CIA is involved: The ICT RMF is the umbrella framework for protecting confidentiality, integrity and availability of ICT systems and data.
items.Evidence to verify: ICT RMF documentation, annual/post-incident review records
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: ICT systems, protocols and tools
items.Requirement: Use ICT systems/protocols/tools that are appropriate to operations, reliable under stress/peak load, technologically resilient, and kept up to date with security standards (patched/maintained).
items.Why CIA is involved: Directly requires reliability (availability), up-to-date security (confidentiality/integrity) and resilience under load.
items.Evidence to verify: Technology standards, patch/maintenance records, capacity/stress-test evidence
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Identification
items.Requirement: Identify and classify ICT-supported functions, ICT and information assets, and all sources of ICT risk; maintain an updated ICT asset inventory, map interdependencies, and identify single points of failure.
items.Why CIA is involved: Knowing what assets exist and where single points of failure sit underpins protection of confidentiality, integrity and availability.
items.Evidence to verify: ICT asset inventory, dependency mapping, single-point-of-failure analysis
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Protection and prevention
items.Requirement: Implement controls: information security policies/procedures/access controls, network segmentation, encryption/cryptography policies, third-party access policies, change management, document management, patch management, and ICT project management policies.
items.Why CIA is involved: The core preventive-control set - access control, segmentation and encryption directly protect confidentiality and integrity; patching protects availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Security policy set, access control, segmentation, encryption, patch and change management evidence
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Detection
items.Requirement: Maintain mechanisms to promptly detect anomalous activities, including ICT network problems and ICT-related incidents, with multiple layers of control and defined alert thresholds/criteria.
items.Why CIA is involved: Detection capability underpins the ability to catch confidentiality, integrity and availability-impacting events early.
items.Evidence to verify: Detection/monitoring tooling, alert thresholds, layered control design
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Response and recovery
items.Requirement: Implement an ICT business continuity policy (activation triggers, recovery priorities, interim procedures, assessment/decision procedures); conduct a business impact analysis with RTOs/RPOs for critical functions; implement response/recovery plans; test business continuity plans at least annually.
items.Why CIA is involved: Business continuity and recovery planning is fundamentally about restoring availability of critical ICT functions after disruption.
items.Evidence to verify: BCP/DR policy, BIA with RTO/RPO, annual BC test results
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Backup policies and procedures
items.Requirement: Maintain backup policies specifying frequency, type and location/scope of backups; keep restoration systems separate from the primary system and activatable without undue delay; test restorability so restore times align with RTOs; cloud-hosted backups are permitted.
items.Why CIA is involved: Backups protect against loss of data integrity and restore availability after an incident.
items.Evidence to verify: Backup policy, restoration testing records aligned to RTO
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Learning and evolving
items.Requirement: Gather, analyse and document findings from major ICT incidents and post-incident reviews; monitor cyber threat intelligence and integrate it into risk assessment; provide ICT security awareness training to all staff, specialist resilience training to relevant roles, and board-level ICT risk training.
items.Why CIA is involved: Learning from incidents and threat intelligence strengthens ongoing protection across confidentiality, integrity and availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Post-incident review records, threat intelligence integration, training records at all levels incl. board
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Communication
items.Requirement: Implement crisis communication plans for major ICT incidents or cyber threats, with defined internal escalation procedures and external communication to clients, sector counterparts and public authorities.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: Simplified ICT risk management framework
items.Requirement: Small and less complex entities may apply a simplified ICT RMF covering key risk-management elements, simplified testing and simplified reporting, per the applicable regulatory technical standards.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Chapter II - ICT risk management (Art.5-16)

items.Title: ICT-related incident management process
items.Requirement: Establish a documented incident management process with defined roles, classification criteria and escalation paths; report major incidents to senior management with the board informed; communicate with affected clients without undue delay.
items.Why CIA is involved: The incident process exists to detect and respond to events impacting confidentiality, integrity or availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Incident management procedure, escalation records, board/senior-management reporting
items._section: Chapter III - ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Art.17-23)

items.Title: Classification of ICT-related incidents and cyber threats
items.Requirement: Classify incidents by impact criteria: clients affected, reputational impact, duration/geographic spread, data losses, service criticality, and economic impact, per the applicable regulatory technical standard.
items.Why CIA is involved: Classification criteria directly reference data loss (confidentiality/integrity) and service criticality (availability).
items.Evidence to verify: Incident classification criteria and classified incident log
items._section: Chapter III - ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Art.17-23)

items.Title: Reporting of major ICT-related incidents
items.Requirement: Report major incidents to the competent authority in three stages: initial notification within 4 hours of classification as major, intermediate update within 72 hours, and final report within one month; voluntary notification of significant cyber threats is permitted.
items.Why CIA is involved: Major-incident reporting is triggered specifically by confidentiality/integrity/availability-impacting events.
items.Evidence to verify: Major-incident notification records against the 4-hour/72-hour/1-month timeline
items._section: Chapter III - ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Art.17-23)

items.Title: Specific rules for payment-related major incidents
items.Requirement: Credit/payment/e-money institutions integrate payment-incident reporting (previously under PSD2) with the DORA major-incident reporting templates and timelines.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Payment-incident reporting process aligned to DORA templates
items._section: Chapter III - ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Art.17-23)

items.Title: General requirements for resilience testing
items.Requirement: Conduct a testing programme for critical ICT systems at least annually, performed by independent internal or external parties.
items.Why CIA is involved: Testing validates that confidentiality, integrity and availability controls actually work as designed.
items.Evidence to verify: Annual testing programme, independence evidence for testers
items._section: Chapter IV - Digital operational resilience testing (Art.24-27)

items.Title: Testing of ICT tools and systems
items.Requirement: Perform a range of basic tests: vulnerability assessments/scans, network security assessments, source code reviews, performance tests, end-to-end tests, and scenario-based compatibility tests.
items.Why CIA is involved: This is the direct technical security/resilience testing regime covering confidentiality, integrity and availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Vulnerability scan, code review, performance and end-to-end test reports
items._section: Chapter IV - Digital operational resilience testing (Art.24-27)

items.Title: Advanced testing based on threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)
items.Requirement: Entities meeting applicability criteria perform TLPT at least every three years, on live production systems, covering critical/important functions, using cyber threat intelligence to develop realistic attack scenarios; results are mutually recognised across EU jurisdictions.
items.Why CIA is involved: TLPT is a live, adversarial test of the organisation's actual resilience against confidentiality, integrity and availability attacks.
items.Evidence to verify: TLPT scope, scenario design based on threat intelligence, TLPT report
items._section: Chapter IV - Digital operational resilience testing (Art.24-27)

items.Title: Requirements for TLPT testers
items.Requirement: Testers must demonstrate methodology capability and technical expertise, hold relevant professional certifications, and have no conflict of interest with the tested entity.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Chapter IV - Digital operational resilience testing (Art.24-27)

items.Title: General principles for managing ICT third-party risk
items.Requirement: Adopt, review and update an ICT third-party risk policy; record all ICT service arrangements in a Register of Information (submitted at least annually to the competent authority); perform pre-contractual due diligence for critical/important functions; monitor TPSP performance and risk on an ongoing basis; assess ICT concentration risk; define an exit strategy for each critical arrangement.
items.Why CIA is involved: Third-party ICT risk directly threatens confidentiality, integrity and availability of outsourced systems/data; concentration risk specifically threatens availability.
items.Evidence to verify: ICT third-party risk policy, Register of Information, due-diligence and monitoring records, exit strategies
items._section: Chapter V S1 - Managing ICT third-party risk - key principles (Art.28-30)

items.Title: Preliminary assessment of ICT concentration risk at entity level
items.Requirement: Assess, before entering a new ICT service arrangement, the entity-level concentration risk, including the risk that entire ICT services could become unavailable due to reliance on a single provider.
items.Why CIA is involved: Concentration risk is specifically about the availability impact of over-reliance on a single ICT provider.
items.Evidence to verify: Concentration-risk assessment per new/renewed ICT arrangement
items._section: Chapter V S1 - Managing ICT third-party risk - key principles (Art.28-30)

items.Title: Key contractual provisions
items.Requirement: Ensure contracts for critical/important functions include mandatory provisions: service description, data locations, data protection, availability/security, audit and access rights, termination rights, reporting, data portability, and sub-contracting terms; lighter provisions apply to non-critical arrangements.
items.Why CIA is involved: The mandated clauses explicitly cover data protection, availability and security - all three CIA properties - in third-party contracts.
items.Evidence to verify: Contract clause checklist against Art.30(2) mandatory provisions
items._section: Chapter V S1 - Managing ICT third-party risk - key principles (Art.28-30)

items.Title: Designation of critical ICT third-party service providers (CTPPs)
items.Requirement: Be aware that the European Supervisory Authorities designate certain ICT third-party providers as 'critical' based on defined criteria; non-EU critical providers must designate an EU legal representative.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Awareness of CTPP status of key providers used
items._section: Chapter V S2 - Oversight of critical ICT third-party service providers (Art.31-44, summary)

items.Title: Liability of financial entities
items.Requirement: Designation of a provider as a CTPP, and the oversight regime around it, does not reduce the financial entity's own responsibility for DORA compliance - obligations cannot be outsourced to the provider.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Internal accountability retained regardless of CTPP oversight status
items._section: Chapter V S2 - Oversight of critical ICT third-party service providers (Art.31-44, summary)

items.Title: Cyber threat information and intelligence sharing
items.Requirement: May voluntarily participate in cyber threat intelligence sharing arrangements with other financial entities, while protecting confidential information and complying with competition rules; participation supports (but does not replace) the threat-intelligence duties under Art.13.
items.Why CIA is involved: Confidential information shared in these arrangements must itself be protected.
items._section: Chapter VI - Information-sharing arrangements (Art.45)

items.Title: Supervisory powers and penalties
items.Requirement: Be aware competent authorities can order cessation of non-compliant conduct, impose administrative penalties (on the entity and responsible natural persons), and publish penalty/measure information (naming and shaming); some Member States also provide criminal penalties.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Legal/compliance risk register reflecting DORA penalty exposure
items._section: Chapters VII-IX - Competent authorities, delegated acts, transitional/final provisions (Art.46-64, summary)

items.Title: Application date
items.Requirement: DORA entered into force 16 January 2023 and has applied from 17 January 2025.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - governance, legal or supervisory-process obligation without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Compliance programme aligned to the 17 January 2025 application date
items._section: Chapters VII-IX - Competent authorities, delegated acts, transitional/final provisions (Art.46-64, summary)

items.Title: Understand ARIA's purpose and scope
items.Practice: Recognize ARIA (Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI) as a NIST AI Innovation Lab testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) research program that measures how AI systems behave in realistic, real-world conditions - not only in controlled benchmarks - across generalizable and context-specific risks.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Internal briefing/awareness note on ARIA's purpose and current pilot (ARIA 0.1, LLM-focused)
items._section: Program - Program fundamentals - understanding what ARIA is (and is not)

items.Title: Understand ARIA is not a certification or compliance programme
items.Practice: Confirm internally that participation or alignment with ARIA does not constitute certification, regulatory compliance, or an official safety approval - it is a research evaluation environment whose results are published for the AI community's benefit.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Internal communication clarifying ARIA is non-certifying
items._section: Program - Program fundamentals - understanding what ARIA is (and is not)

items.Title: Map ARIA to the NIST AI RMF and GenAI Profile already in use
items.Practice: Confirm how ARIA builds on and operationalizes the NIST AI RMF (Tab 5) and the risks identified in the GenAI Profile (NIST AI 600-1), so ARIA engagement reuses existing AI RMF risk-management work rather than duplicating it.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Cross-reference between ARIA engagement plan and existing AI RMF Measure function (Tab 5) outputs
items._section: Program - Program fundamentals - understanding what ARIA is (and is not)

items.Title: Prepare systems/documentation to support model-testing claims
items.Practice: Ensure claimed capabilities, intended use and performance characteristics of the AI system/model are documented clearly enough to be verified in a model-testing evaluation.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Model card / capability documentation ready for independent verification
items._section: Model Testing - Level 1 - Model testing (confirm claimed capabilities)

items.Title: Align model testing with the 'secure and resilient' trustworthy characteristic
items.Practice: Where model testing covers security-relevant behaviour (robustness to adversarial inputs, resistance to manipulation), ensure this is explicitly scoped alongside functional/accuracy testing.
items.Why CIA is involved: Model-level security/robustness testing verifies the system resists confidentiality, integrity and availability-impacting manipulation.
items.Evidence to verify: Test plan explicitly covering security/robustness alongside accuracy benchmarks
items._section: Model Testing - Level 1 - Model testing (confirm claimed capabilities)

items.Title: Establish or engage a red-teaming capability aligned to ARIA's approach
items.Practice: Build (or contract) a red-teaming capability able to rigorously challenge the AI system to surface weaknesses, consistent with ARIA's structured, scenario-based red-teaming methodology.
items.Why CIA is involved: Red teaming is explicitly adversarial security testing aimed at inducing confidentiality, integrity and availability-impacting failures.
items.Evidence to verify: Red-team charter/engagement scoped to ARIA-style structured adversarial testing
items._section: Red Teaming - Level 2 - Red teaming (stress test and attempt to induce risks)

items.Title: Scope red-teaming scenarios against known AI risk taxonomies
items.Practice: Design red-team scenarios informed by the NIST AI RMF GenAI Profile risks and, where relevant, the OWASP LLM Top 10 (Tab 10), so red-teaming coverage is traceable to a recognized risk set.
items.Why CIA is involved: Scenario-based adversarial testing against known attack patterns directly probes confidentiality, integrity and availability weaknesses.
items.Evidence to verify: Red-team scenario catalogue mapped to GenAI Profile risks and/or OWASP LLM Top 10
items._section: Red Teaming - Level 2 - Red teaming (stress test and attempt to induce risks)

items.Title: Capture and remediate red-team findings
items.Practice: Document red-teaming findings, prioritise by severity, and track remediation to closure, consistent with how ARIA expects materialized risks to feed back into system improvement.
items.Why CIA is involved: Tracking findings to closure preserves the integrity of the risk-remediation process.
items.Evidence to verify: Red-team findings log and remediation tracker
items._section: Red Teaming - Level 2 - Red teaming (stress test and attempt to induce risks)

items.Title: Plan for human-AI interaction evaluation under realistic conditions
items.Practice: Where feasible, evaluate the AI system under conditions resembling real-world use by diverse users/testers, not only synthetic benchmark prompts, to surface context-dependent risks.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Field-testing or pilot-use evaluation plan with diverse real-world scenarios
items._section: Field Testing - Level 3 - Field testing (examine impacts under regular use)

items.Title: Assess both positive and negative impacts arising from regular use
items.Practice: Examine impacts the AI system has in practice - beneficial and harmful - on the people and groups who interact with it, feeding results back into the AI System Impact Assessment (Tab 6, ISO 42005) and AI RMF Map function (Tab 5).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Field-testing impact findings cross-referenced to the ISO 42005 impact assessment
items._section: Field Testing - Level 3 - Field testing (examine impacts under regular use)

items.Title: Understand CoRIx as ARIA's composite measurement instrument
items.Practice: Recognize that ARIA scores evaluated systems on the Contextual Robustness Index (CoRIx), a suite of metrics (ARIA documents ten measurement dimensions, including the seven AI RMF trustworthy characteristics - valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable/interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed) indicating whether a system maintains trustworthy functionality across varied deployment conditions.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Internal summary of CoRIx dimensions relevant to the organization's AI systems
items._section: Measurement - Measurement layer - Contextual Robustness Index (CoRIx) and related metrics

items.Title: Track the 'secure and resilient' CoRIx dimension specifically
items.Practice: Within the broader CoRIx scoring, give explicit attention to the secure-and-resilient dimension as the one most directly tied to cybersecurity outcomes, and ensure it is measured with the same rigour as validity/reliability.
items.Why CIA is involved: This CoRIx dimension is explicitly the security dimension of the index, covering resilience to attack and manipulation across confidentiality, integrity and availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Dimension-level tracking of secure/resilient scores from any ARIA-aligned evaluation
items._section: Measurement - Measurement layer - Contextual Robustness Index (CoRIx) and related metrics

items.Title: Follow ARIA's data and evaluation-rules requirements if participating
items.Practice: If submitting a system/application for ARIA evaluation, confirm the organization can comply with NIST's stated evaluation rules and data-handling expectations (e.g. data collected is used for research purposes per the published ARIA Data/Evaluation policies).
items.Why CIA is involved: Data submitted into a third-party research evaluation environment needs confidentiality safeguards appropriate to its sensitivity.
items.Evidence to verify: Review of current ARIA participation/data-handling terms before submission (check ai-challenges.nist.gov/aria for the latest)
items._section: Data & Participation - Data handling and participation in ARIA evaluations

items.Title: Treat ARIA results as research input, not a compliance record
items.Practice: Use published ARIA evaluation outcomes (where available) as additional evidence to strengthen internal AI RMF Measure/Manage activities (Tab 5), not as a substitute for the organization's own risk assessment, impact assessment, or regulatory compliance work.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - research/evaluation-engagement practice without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Internal note on how ARIA outcomes feed into, but do not replace, existing risk/impact assessments
items._section: Data & Participation - Data handling and participation in ARIA evaluations

items.Title: Risk (top-level definition)
items.Requirement: Define risk as the probable frequency and probable magnitude of future loss, derived by combining Loss Event Frequency (LEF) and Probable Loss Magnitude (PLM) - not a subjective high/medium/low label.
items.Why CIA is involved: FAIR risk scenarios are ultimately about the frequency and magnitude of loss arising from confidentiality, integrity and/or availability-impacting events.
items.Evidence to verify: Risk scenario statements expressed as LEF x PLM rather than qualitative ratings
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Loss Event Frequency (LEF)
items.Requirement: Define LEF as the probable frequency, within a given timeframe, that a threat agent will inflict harm upon an asset - derived from Threat Event Frequency and Vulnerability.
items.Why CIA is involved: LEF estimates how often a CIA-impacting loss event is expected to occur.
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Threat Event Frequency (TEF)
items.Requirement: Define TEF as the probable frequency, within a given timeframe, that a threat agent will act against an asset - derived from Contact Frequency and Probability of Action.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: TEF estimate with contact-frequency and probability-of-action inputs documented
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Threat Capability (TCap)
items.Requirement: Define TCap as the probable level of force a threat agent is capable of applying against an asset (skill and resources).
items.Why CIA is involved: Assessing an attacker's capability to overcome controls is directly about the likelihood of a confidentiality/integrity/availability compromise.
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Resistance Strength / Control Strength (RS/CS)
items.Requirement: Define Resistance Strength as the expected effectiveness of controls, measured against a baseline level of force, in preventing a threat agent from succeeding.
items.Why CIA is involved: Control strength is literally the measure of how well existing security controls resist confidentiality/integrity/availability compromise.
items.Evidence to verify: Control strength estimate for the controls protecting the asset in scope
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Vulnerability (Vuln)
items.Requirement: Derive Vulnerability as the probability that a threat event becomes a loss event, by comparing Threat Capability against Resistance Strength.
items.Why CIA is involved: Vulnerability is the probability that an attack actually succeeds in compromising confidentiality, integrity or availability.
items.Evidence to verify: Vulnerability derivation combining TCap and RS/CS estimates
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Probable Loss Magnitude (PLM) and the six forms of loss
items.Requirement: Estimate PLM by combining Primary Loss (direct impact to the organization) and Secondary Loss (impact from secondary stakeholder reactions, e.g. regulators, customers), categorised across the six forms of loss: productivity, response, replacement, fines and judgments, competitive advantage, and reputation.
items.Why CIA is involved: Loss magnitude is the direct business consequence of confidentiality, integrity or availability-impacting events materialising.
items.Evidence to verify: PLM worksheet covering primary and secondary loss across all six loss forms
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Secondary Loss Event Frequency and Magnitude
items.Requirement: Where secondary stakeholders are likely to react (e.g. regulatory notification, customer churn, litigation), estimate the probability of that secondary reaction and its own magnitude separately from primary loss.
items.Why CIA is involved: Secondary loss is frequently triggered by a confidentiality breach (e.g. data exposure) prompting regulatory or customer reaction.
items.Evidence to verify: Secondary loss estimate with reaction probability and magnitude
items._section: Taxonomy - FAIR core risk taxonomy (the factors to define before analysing any scenario)

items.Title: Stage 1 / Step 1 - Identify the asset at risk
items.Requirement: Clearly identify and scope the specific asset (data, system, process) that is the subject of the risk scenario, at a level of granularity that supports meaningful analysis.
items.Why CIA is involved: The asset-at-risk identification frames which confidentiality, integrity and availability properties are actually being analysed.
items.Evidence to verify: Documented asset-at-risk definition per scenario, linked to the organization's asset inventory
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 1 / Step 2 - Identify the threat community
items.Requirement: Identify and characterise the threat community under consideration (e.g. external cybercriminals, malicious insiders, non-malicious/human error, nation-state actors) relevant to the asset and scenario.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 2 / Step 3 - Estimate Threat Event Frequency
items.Requirement: Estimate the probable frequency of threat-agent action against the asset, using calibrated estimation (ranges with confidence levels) rather than single-point guesses.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Calibrated TEF estimate with supporting rationale/data sources
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 2 / Step 4 - Estimate Threat Capability
items.Requirement: Estimate the probable skill and resource level of the threat community relative to a defined scale.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 2 / Step 5 - Estimate Control/Resistance Strength
items.Requirement: Estimate the strength of controls protecting the asset against the threat community in scope, calibrated against the same scale used for Threat Capability.
items.Why CIA is involved: This step directly measures how well implemented security controls resist confidentiality/integrity/availability compromise.
items.Evidence to verify: Calibrated control-strength estimate referencing actual control implementation (e.g. from ISO 27001 Annex A controls already tracked in this workbook)
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 2 / Step 6 - Derive Vulnerability
items.Requirement: Combine Threat Capability and Control Strength estimates (e.g. via a calibrated lookup table or Monte Carlo simulation) to derive the probability that a threat event becomes a loss event.
items.Why CIA is involved: Directly expresses the probability of a successful confidentiality/integrity/availability compromise.
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 2 / Step 7 - Derive Loss Event Frequency
items.Requirement: Combine Threat Event Frequency and Vulnerability to derive the probable frequency of actual loss events for the scenario.
items.Why CIA is involved: LEF is the quantified frequency of CIA-impacting loss events.
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 3 / Step 8 - Estimate worst-case loss
items.Requirement: Estimate the worst reasonably foreseeable loss magnitude for the scenario, as a bounding reference point.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 3 / Step 9 - Estimate probable loss magnitude
items.Requirement: Estimate the probable (most likely range of) loss magnitude for the scenario, considering primary and secondary loss across the six forms of loss (see T.7-T.8).
items.Why CIA is involved: The loss magnitude quantifies the business impact of confidentiality, integrity or availability compromise.
items.Evidence to verify: Probable loss magnitude estimate (distribution) per scenario
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Stage 4 / Step 10 - Derive and articulate risk
items.Requirement: Combine the Loss Event Frequency and Probable Loss Magnitude distributions (typically via Monte Carlo simulation) to produce a risk result - e.g. a loss exceedance curve or annualized loss expectancy range - and communicate it in business terms.
items.Why CIA is involved: The final quantified risk result represents the combined confidentiality/integrity/availability risk exposure in business terms.
items.Evidence to verify: Risk model output (loss exceedance curve / ALE range) and executive-level risk articulation
items._section: Process - The four-stage, ten-step FAIR risk assessment process

items.Title: Use calibrated estimation techniques
items.Requirement: Train analysts in calibrated estimation (e.g. the 90% confidence-interval calibration training common in FAIR practice) so subjective range estimates are statistically defensible rather than arbitrary.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Calibration training records for risk analysts
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: Maintain a consistent FAIR taxonomy and glossary
items.Requirement: Ensure all analysts use the same FAIR definitions (per the FAIR taxonomy standard, e.g. Open FAIR O-RT) so risk scenarios are comparable across the organization and over time.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: Use a repeatable analysis process with peer review
items.Requirement: Apply the four-stage/ten-step process consistently, with peer review of estimates and model outputs before they are reported to decision-makers.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: FAIR analysis workflow with peer-review sign-off
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: Select and maintain appropriate tooling
items.Requirement: Use a FAIR-conformant tool (e.g. the Open Group's Open FAIR Risk Analysis tool, FAIR-U, RiskLens, or an equivalent Monte Carlo-capable model) rather than ad hoc spreadsheets lacking distribution-based simulation.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Approved FAIR tooling and version/configuration record
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: Integrate FAIR outputs into the existing risk register and decision processes
items.Requirement: Feed FAIR-quantified risk scenarios into the organization's existing risk register, risk appetite statements, and treatment decisions (e.g. alongside the ISO 27001/42001 risk registers already tracked in this workbook), rather than running FAIR as an isolated exercise.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Cross-reference from FAIR scenario outputs to the organization's risk register and treatment plan
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: Validate the methodology periodically against the Open Group's requirements for risk assessment methodologies
items.Requirement: Periodically check that the organization's FAIR implementation still satisfies the general quality criteria for a sound risk methodology (clearly defined, internally consistent taxonomy; ability to express variability/uncertainty with ranges and distributions; logically defensible relationships between factors; and results that support meaningful comparison and prioritisation across scenarios).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - methodological/organizational rigor requirement without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Periodic internal review of FAIR implementation against these quality criteria
items._section: Governance - Organizational requirements to implement FAIR correctly

items.Title: ISO/IEC 5181 - identification
items.Requirement / Guidance: Title: 'Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Data provenance'. Developed by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 (Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection), ICS 35.030. Status at time of writing: International Standard under publication (final production), expected publication around October 2026 - check ISO's site for the confirmed publication date and edition before relying on this tab for formal audit evidence.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - terminology/application-mapping item without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Status - Standard identification and status (verified from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27)

items.Title: Official scope / abstract
items.Requirement / Guidance: Verified scope: 'This document provides guidelines, methodology and techniques for deriving securely information denoted to as provenance metadata about data assets from multiple sources, intermediaries or users.' - i.e. how to capture, derive and secure provenance metadata across a data asset's chain of custody, not specific to AI but directly applicable to AI training/operational data and model lineage.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - terminology/application-mapping item without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Scope statement on file for audit-readiness context
items._section: Status - Standard identification and status (verified from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27)

items.Title: Provenance concepts and terminology
items.Requirement / Guidance: Establish and apply consistent definitions of provenance-related terms (provenance, provenance metadata, data asset, intermediary, actor, chain of custody) so provenance records are comparable and interoperable.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - terminology/application-mapping item without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Provenance metadata model
items.Requirement / Guidance: Define what provenance metadata is captured for a data asset: originating source, each actor/intermediary that touched the data, timestamps, transformations/processing applied, and the context of each step.
items.Why CIA is involved: A well-defined metadata model is the basis for an accurate, tamper-evident record of what happened to a data asset - an integrity concern.
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Secure derivation and recording of provenance
items.Requirement / Guidance: Apply security techniques (e.g. cryptographic signing, hashing, tamper-evident logging) so provenance metadata itself can be trusted and is not subject to undetected alteration.
items.Why CIA is involved: This is the standard's core security contribution: deriving provenance 'securely' means protecting the confidentiality of sensitive provenance details and the integrity of the provenance record itself.
items.Evidence to verify: Cryptographic/tamper-evidence controls applied to provenance records
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Provenance across multiple sources, intermediaries and users
items.Requirement / Guidance: Capture and preserve provenance information as a data asset moves across multiple organizations, systems or individuals, maintaining an unbroken, attributable chain of custody.
items.Why CIA is involved: An unbroken chain of custody across parties is fundamentally an integrity property of the provenance record.
items.Evidence to verify: Multi-party provenance chain documentation (e.g. for data passed through suppliers, data brokers, or federated AI training)
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Provenance assurance and trust levels
items.Requirement / Guidance: Assess and communicate the level of assurance/trust that can be placed in a given provenance record, based on how it was derived and secured (e.g. self-asserted vs cryptographically verified).
items.Why CIA is involved: Trust/assurance levels help determine who can rely on provenance claims, which relates to confidentiality of the underlying trust decisions.
items.Evidence to verify: Provenance assurance-level classification applied to key datasets
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Provenance record availability and retention
items.Requirement / Guidance: Maintain provenance records in a way that keeps them available and retrievable for as long as the data asset (or its derivatives, e.g. a trained AI model) remains in use.
items.Why CIA is involved: If provenance records become unavailable, the chain of custody cannot be verified when needed - an availability concern.
