items.Evidence to verify: Provenance record retention policy aligned to data/model lifecycle
items._section: Topical - Topical structure (inferred from scope and SC27 provenance-standard conventions - NOT verified numbered clauses; confirm against the published text)

items.Title: Training and operational dataset provenance
items.Requirement / Guidance: Apply ISO/IEC 5181's provenance techniques to datasets used for AI training, fine-tuning, RAG/retrieval and evaluation, recording source, collection method, licensing and every transformation the dataset underwent before use.
items.Why CIA is involved: Securely derived dataset provenance protects against undetected data poisoning (integrity) and can reveal sensitive source information needing confidentiality protection.
items.Evidence to verify: Dataset provenance records cross-referenced to the Data Governance Register (Tab 19) and ISO 42001 A.7.5 (Tabs 1-2)
items._section: AI - Application to AI data and AI system provenance

items.Title: Model lineage and versioning provenance
items.Requirement / Guidance: Record the provenance of the AI model itself: base model(s) used, fine-tuning datasets and steps applied, version history, and who/what performed each step - distinct from but complementary to the data-level provenance in AI.1.
items.Why CIA is involved: Model lineage integrity underpins trust that a deployed model is the one that was actually tested and approved.
items.Evidence to verify: Model card / model lineage register with provenance metadata per version
items._section: AI - Application to AI data and AI system provenance

items.Title: Provenance for third-party and supply-chain AI components
items.Requirement / Guidance: Extend provenance capture to third-party models, datasets, libraries and APIs incorporated into an AI system, consistent with the AI supply-chain controls already tracked elsewhere in this workbook (ISO 42001 A.10, Tab 1-2; EU AI Act value-chain provisions, Tab 3).
items.Why CIA is involved: Unverified third-party component provenance is a known AI supply-chain attack vector (see OWASP LLM03 Supply Chain, Tab 10).
items._section: AI - Application to AI data and AI system provenance

items.Title: Provenance of AI-generated content (related but distinct standard)
items.Requirement / Guidance: Where the AI system generates synthetic content (text, image, audio, video), be aware that content-level provenance/authenticity (e.g. watermarking, C2PA Content Credentials) is addressed by separate, content-focused standards/initiatives rather than by ISO/IEC 5181 itself, which is scoped to data-asset provenance; apply both where relevant.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - terminology/application-mapping item without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Mapping of which provenance mechanism (ISO/IEC 5181 for data assets vs C2PA-style content credentials for generated outputs) applies to each AI use case
items._section: AI - Application to AI data and AI system provenance

items.Title: Integration with existing AI governance clauses
items.Requirement / Guidance: Use ISO/IEC 5181 as the detailed 'how' for provenance behind the 'what' already required elsewhere: ISO 42001 A.7.5 (data provenance), EU AI Act Art.10 (data governance), GDPR Art.5(1)(f)/30 (integrity/confidentiality principle, records of processing), and the NIST AI RMF Map function (Tab 5).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - terminology/application-mapping item without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Cross-reference table linking ISO/IEC 5181 provenance techniques to each framework's provenance-related clause
items._section: AI - Application to AI data and AI system provenance

items.Title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 - identification
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Title: 'Cybersecurity - Artificial Intelligence - Addressing security threats and compromises to AI systems'. First edition, published October 2026 by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27/WG 4 (development started 2022). Draws on ISO/IEC 22989 (AI concepts/terminology), ISO/IEC 5338 (AI system life cycle), ISO/IEC 42001 (AIMS) and ISO/IEC 38507 (governance implications of AI for the body governing the organization).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - scope/governance framing without a direct CIA-protection function.
items._section: Status - Standard identification (verified)

items.Title: Official scope and framing
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Guides organizations on addressing security threats to AI systems: discusses organisational consequences of security threats compromising AI systems at various life-cycle points, and explains how to detect and mitigate them. Scope is threats TO AI systems of concern to the AI system owner - not threats INVOLVING AI used by attackers against others, and excludes AI-vs-AI 'robot wars' scenarios.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - scope/governance framing without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Scope statement on file; AI threat-model boundary agreed (owner's AI system, not AI misuse by third parties)
items._section: Status - Standard identification (verified)

items.Title: Apply established information security practice as the foundation
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Recognize that AI systems run on conventional computer systems/networks, so all the usual confidentiality, integrity and availability/cybersecurity concerns (e.g. ISO 27001/27002, Tab 7) still apply and remain essential - AI-specific threats are additive, not a replacement.
items.Why CIA is involved: This clause is explicit that conventional CIA/cybersecurity practice is the necessary foundation beneath AI-specific threat handling.
items.Evidence to verify: Confirmation that existing ISMS controls (Tab 7) are applied to AI system infrastructure before layering AI-specific controls
items._section: Clause 5 - Application of information security

items.Title: Address governance, management and procedural dimensions
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Treat AI security as spanning strategic, tactical and operational levels - design, development, testing, implementation/integration, use, monitoring, management, maintenance and eventual decommissioning of the AI system - not only technical/CIA controls.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - scope/governance framing without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: AI security governance structure spanning the full life cycle (cross-reference ISO 42001, Tabs 1-2, and ISO/IEC 5338 life-cycle stages)
items._section: Clause 5 - Application of information security

items.Title: Data poisoning
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Deliberate injection of false, mislabelled or manipulated data into training/fine-tuning data to corrupt the resulting model's behaviour.
items.Why CIA is involved: Poisoning is a direct attack on the integrity of the model's learned behaviour via its training data.
items.Evidence to verify: Data provenance/integrity controls on training data (cross-ref Tab 19 Data Governance Register, Tab 20 ISO 5181)
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Model poisoning
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Deliberate manipulation of the model itself (e.g. during training, fine-tuning, or via a compromised supply-chain component) to embed a backdoor or degrade behaviour.
items.Why CIA is involved: Model poisoning directly corrupts the integrity of the deployed model.
items.Evidence to verify: Model training pipeline integrity controls, signed/verified model artifacts
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Evasion
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Deliberately crafted training or prompt inputs designed to mislead the AI algorithm at inference time (adversarial examples, adversarial prompts).
items.Why CIA is involved: Evasion attacks manipulate model output/behaviour without authorization - an integrity compromise.
items.Evidence to verify: Adversarial robustness testing (cross-ref OWASP LLM01 Prompt Injection, Tab 10)
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Membership inference
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Techniques to determine whether a specific data point was part of a model's training data, potentially revealing sensitive information about individuals in the training set.
items.Why CIA is involved: Membership inference is a confidentiality attack - it reveals information about the training data that should not be inferable.
items.Evidence to verify: Membership-inference testing as part of model privacy/security evaluation
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Model inversion
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Techniques to reconstruct or infer characteristics of training data points from a model's outputs or parameters, potentially recovering sensitive underlying data.
items.Why CIA is involved: Model inversion directly threatens confidentiality of the underlying training data.
items.Evidence to verify: Model inversion resistance testing (e.g. output perturbation, differential privacy)
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Model stealing (extraction)
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Theft of the valuable intellectual property embodied in a trained model - the model itself, its training data, and its inputs/prompts - typically via systematic querying.
items.Why CIA is involved: Model stealing is a confidentiality/IP-theft attack against the model and the data embodied within it.
items.Evidence to verify: Rate limiting, query monitoring and IP-protection controls (cross-ref OWASP LLM10 Unbounded Consumption, Tab 10)
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Prompt injection and output injection
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Downstream attacks exploiting vulnerabilities in operational AI systems: injecting malicious instructions via prompts, or injecting malicious content via the model's output into systems that consume it.
items.Why CIA is involved: Prompt/output injection can be used to exfiltrate data (C), manipulate downstream behaviour (I), or trigger disruptive actions (A) depending on what the output feeds into.
items.Evidence to verify: Input/output validation and sanitization controls (cross-ref OWASP LLM01/LLM05, Tab 10)
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Further threats per the standard's catalogue (12+ scenarios)
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Beyond the named threats above, the standard's threat catalogue covers at least a dozen scenarios in total (each with about a page of guidance); review the full published catalogue for scenarios not individually itemised in this tab (e.g. supply-chain-specific variants, denial-of-service against AI inference, and other emerging attack patterns).
items.Why CIA is involved: None - scope/governance framing without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Full threat-catalogue review against the published ISO/IEC 27090 text
items._section: Clause 6 - Types of potential compromise to AI systems (threat catalogue)

items.Title: Apply threat-specific detection and mitigation guidance
items.Requirement / Threat Description: For each threat in Clause 6, apply the standard's guidance on characterising the threat, its potential consequences, and how to detect and mitigate it - rather than applying generic security controls uniformly without considering threat-specific nuances.
items.Why CIA is involved: Threat-specific mitigation is how the standard operationalizes protecting confidentiality, integrity and availability against each distinct AI attack pattern.
items.Evidence to verify: Threat-by-threat mitigation mapping (one control set per threat type in Clause 6)
items._section: Clause 7 - Mitigations and their interactions with threats

items.Title: Consider interactions between mitigations and threats
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Assess how a mitigation applied for one threat may interact with (help, hinder, or be neutral to) other threats and other already-applied mitigations, avoiding a false sense of security from mitigations that only address a single threat in isolation.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - scope/governance framing without a direct CIA-protection function.
items.Evidence to verify: Documented mitigation-interaction analysis across the threat catalogue
items._section: Clause 7 - Mitigations and their interactions with threats

items.Title: Mapping attacks to AI system life cycle and assets
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Map each threat/attack to the specific AI system life-cycle stage(s) (per ISO/IEC 5338) and asset(s) it targets (data, model, infrastructure, prompts/outputs), to prioritise controls at the stages and assets most exposed.
items.Why CIA is involved: Mapping attacks to life-cycle stage and asset is how the standard targets confidentiality, integrity and availability protection where it is actually needed.
items.Evidence to verify: Life-cycle and asset mapping completed for the organization's AI systems (cross-ref ISO 42001 A.4.2-A.4.6, Tabs 1-2)
items._section: Clause 7 - Mitigations and their interactions with threats

items.Title: AI-specific versions of conventional attacks
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Recognize that many conventional cybersecurity attack patterns (e.g. supply-chain compromise, denial of service, credential theft) have AI-specific variants, and apply conventional security knowledge adapted to the AI context rather than treating AI threats as entirely novel.
items.Why CIA is involved: AI-specific variants of conventional attacks still ultimately threaten confidentiality, integrity and availability, consistent with their conventional counterparts.
items.Evidence to verify: Conventional attack catalogue reviewed for AI-specific variants relevant to the organization's systems
items._section: Clause 7 - Mitigations and their interactions with threats

items.Title: Federated machine learning
items.Requirement / Threat Description: Apply additional considerations for federated learning architectures, where training occurs across distributed data holders without centralising raw data - a different trust and attack-surface model from centralised training.
items.Why CIA is involved: Federated learning changes where confidentiality and integrity risks concentrate (at each participant and in the aggregation step) compared with centralised training.
items.Evidence to verify: Federated learning threat model and controls, where this architecture is used
items._section: Clause 7 - Mitigations and their interactions with threats

items.Adversary objective / Description: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems): a public, living knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and real-world case studies targeting AI/ML systems, maintained by MITRE (with the Center for Threat-Informed Defense and industry contributors, incl. the 'Secure AI' initiative). Structured identically to MITRE ATT&CK - tactics as the adversary's objectives (columns), techniques beneath each as the methods to achieve them (rows), each linked to documented mitigations and real-world case studies. Current public release spans 16 tactics and roughly 100+ techniques/sub-techniques, continuing to expand with agentic-AI and multi-agent techniques.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - preparatory/informational tactic without a direct CIA-protection function at this stage.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: ATLAS version/release confirmed against atlas.mitre.org before relying on counts for formal reporting
items._section: Status - Framework identification (verified)

items.Tactic / Topic: How this framework is used (not a compliance checklist)
items.Adversary objective / Description: ATLAS is a threat-intelligence and red-teaming reference, not a certifiable requirements standard: use it to red-team AI systems, to structure detection engineering/SOC use cases for AI-specific attacks, and as a common language between red and blue teams - cross-walk the matrix against your own AI architecture rather than treating every tactic/technique as a mandatory control.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - preparatory/informational tactic without a direct CIA-protection function at this stage.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: AI red-team programme and detection-engineering backlog referencing ATLAS tactics/techniques
items._section: Status - Framework identification (verified)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary gathers information about the target AI/ML system to plan the attack: system capabilities, system prompts, access controls, data sources, competitive/proprietary details.
items.Why CIA is involved: Reconnaissance is fundamentally about extracting information that should remain confidential (system design, prompts, access structure).
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Test for prompt/system-prompt extraction, RBAC enumeration, and disclosure of proprietary or competitive information
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary creates, purchases or compromises resources (malicious prompts, tools, infrastructure) to support the attack - a preparatory stage before the target system is touched.
items.Why CIA is involved: None - preparatory/informational tactic without a direct CIA-protection function at this stage.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Threat intelligence monitoring for adversary tooling/infrastructure relevant to the organization's AI systems
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary gains an initial foothold in the AI/ML system via entry vectors such as input validation weaknesses, prompt injection, SQL/shell injection, SSRF, or exposed debug endpoints.
items.Why CIA is involved: Initial access is the breach point that opens the door to confidentiality, integrity and availability compromise downstream.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Input validation testing, prompt-injection testing, debug-endpoint exposure checks (cross-ref OWASP LLM01, Tab 10)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary obtains some level of access to the AI model itself - ranging from full internal knowledge (white-box) to only inference-API access (black-box) - which shapes what further attacks are feasible.
items.Why CIA is involved: The level of access to model internals is itself a confidentiality property that determines the attacker's subsequent capability.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Model access-boundary review: confirm what level of model access is exposed to which parties
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary runs malicious code or logic within the AI system's environment (e.g. via a compromised pipeline, notebook, or tool invocation).
items.Why CIA is involved: Unauthorized execution directly corrupts the integrity of the system's intended operation.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Execution-environment hardening and monitoring for unauthorized code/command execution in AI pipelines
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary maintains a foothold across restarts, retraining or redeployment of the AI system (e.g. a persistent backdoor embedded in a model or pipeline).
items.Why CIA is involved: Persistence mechanisms are unauthorized, unintended footholds that compromise the integrity of the system over time.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Model/pipeline integrity verification across retraining and redeployment cycles
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary gains higher-level permissions than originally obtained, e.g. escalating from inference-API access to pipeline or infrastructure control.
items.Why CIA is involved: Escalated privileges can be used to compromise confidentiality, integrity and availability depending on what the elevated access reaches.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Least-privilege review of AI pipeline/service accounts and escalation-path testing
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary avoids detection or conceals malicious actions within the AI system, making them appear as normal behaviour (e.g. subtle poisoning below detection thresholds).
items.Why CIA is involved: Evasion undermines the integrity of the organization's ability to trust its own monitoring and detection signal.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Detection-threshold review and anomaly-detection tuning for subtle/low-and-slow AI-specific manipulation
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary steals account names, passwords, API keys or tokens used to access AI systems/services.
items.Why CIA is involved: Credential theft is a direct confidentiality compromise of the access-control mechanism.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Credential/secret-management review for AI pipeline and inference-API access (cross-ref ISO 27001 8.2/8.5, Tab 7)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary maps the AI environment - available models, datasets, tools, APIs and their configuration - to plan further action.
items.Why CIA is involved: Discovery reveals the environment's structure, a confidentiality exposure that enables more targeted follow-on attacks.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Environment/asset exposure review for AI-related infrastructure discoverable by an attacker
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary moves from the initially compromised component to other parts of the AI system or connected environment (e.g. from an agent's tool access into a connected backend system).
items.Why CIA is involved: Lateral movement expands the attacker's reach across systems, multiplying confidentiality, integrity and availability exposure.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Network/service segmentation testing between AI components and the broader environment (cross-ref ISO 27001 8.22, Tab 7)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary gathers data of interest from the AI system - training data, user inputs, outputs, or embeddings - in preparation for exfiltration or further use.
items.Why CIA is involved: Collection is the staging of a confidentiality breach - gathering sensitive data before it leaves the environment.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Data access logging and anomalous-collection-pattern monitoring around AI data stores
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary prepares and positions an AI-specific attack: poisoning inputs/training data, crafting adversarial examples, embedding backdoors, or inducing hallucinations for exploitation - the tactic with the most AI-native techniques and no direct ATT&CK equivalent.
items.Why CIA is involved: Attack staging is specifically about manipulating the AI system's behaviour or training - an integrity attack by nature.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Adversarial-input and data-poisoning testing (cross-ref OWASP LLM01/LLM04/LLM06, Tab 10, and ISO 27090 Clause 6, Tab 21)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary establishes a channel to communicate with and control a compromised AI component remotely.
items.Why CIA is involved: A live command-and-control channel gives the adversary ongoing control that threatens the availability/integrity of the compromised component.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Egress monitoring and anomalous outbound-connection detection from AI infrastructure
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary steals data out of the AI system - PII, training data, proprietary prompts, or other sensitive information - including via encoded/obfuscated channels to evade data-loss prevention.
items.Why CIA is involved: Exfiltration is the direct, final confidentiality breach - sensitive data actually leaving the organization's control.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: DLP tuned for AI-specific exfiltration channels (inference responses, encoded outputs) (cross-ref ISO 27001 8.12, Tab 7)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

items.Adversary objective / Description: Adversary disrupts, degrades, destroys the AI system or manipulates its outputs - hijacking its purpose, generating harmful content, causing unauthorized actions, or taking excessive agency.
items.Why CIA is involved: Impact is the adversary's end goal and can manifest as any combination of confidentiality, integrity or availability compromise.
items.Defensive evidence / test guidance: Impact-scenario red-teaming: hijacking, excessive-agency and output-manipulation testing (cross-ref OWASP LLM06, Tab 10)
items._section: Tactics - The 16 ATLAS tactics (adversary objectives across the attack lifecycle)

paragraphs: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AIMS) - CIA-Security vs Remaining Controls Checklist
Scope: Clauses 4-10 (32 items) and Annex A (38 controls), segregated into two working sheets so security effort is clearly separated from the rest.

Sheet 1 - CIA-Security Controls: items whose primary purpose is to protect the Confidentiality, Integrity or Availability of information/AI assets (data, models, code, infrastructure, logs, documented information). Columns C / I / A show which property each item protects. These need security ownership (CISO/security architecture) and technical evidence.

Sheet 2 - Non-CIA (Other) Controls: governance, leadership, risk planning (general), impact assessment on individuals/society, fairness/ethics, transparency, competence, documentation, performance evaluation, improvement. Owned by AI governance, compliance, legal, HR, product. Column F notes where an item still enables security indirectly.

Judgement rule: an item is CIA-security only if a failure of the requirement would directly expose AI assets to unauthorized access/disclosure (C), unauthorized alteration/poisoning/loss of trustworthiness (I), or loss of access/service (A). Privacy/lawfulness of data use is treated as governance unless the requirement itself is about protecting the data.
The classification is expert judgement for audit planning, not part of the standard. Adjust to your risk assessment; move a row between sheets if your context requires.

How to use: set 'Applicable (SoA)', track 'Status', assign Owner, note gaps. Clauses 4-10 are mandatory; Annex A exclusions need justification (clause 6.1.3). Requirement text is a condensed paraphrase - verify against ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Annex B guidance).
Counts: CIA-security = 18 items; Non-CIA = 52 items; total = 70.

Tab 3 - EU AI Act: 34 articles/annex items relevant to security governance and high-risk AI compliance, of which 12 are marked CIA-security (mainly Art.15 Accuracy/Robustness/Cybersecurity, Art.9 risk management, Art.10 data governance, Art.12/19 logging, Art.26 deployer logging/monitoring, Art.55 GPAI systemic-risk cybersecurity, Art.72 post-market monitoring, Art.73 incident reporting).

Tab 4 - OECD AI Principles (updated May 2024): 14 items across the 5 values-based principles, 5 policy recommendations and 4 update focus areas, of which 3 are marked CIA-security (mainly 1.4 Robustness, security and safety, plus 1.2 privacy and 1.5 accountability/traceability).

Tab 5 - NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST.AI.100-1): 19 categories across GOVERN (6), MAP (5), MEASURE (4) and MANAGE (4) - the framework's full structure is 19 categories / 72 subcategories; this tab tracks at category level. 6 categories are marked CIA-security (Govern 6, Map 4 and Manage 3 - third-party/supply-chain risk; Measure 2 - secure & resilient testing; Measure 3 - risk tracking/monitoring; Manage 4 - incident response and recovery). Suggested actions are condensed from the AI RMF Playbook; verify against NIST.AI.100-1 and the Playbook for subcategory-level detail.

Tab 6 - ISO/IEC 42005:2025 (AI System Impact Assessment guidance): 21 items covering Clause 5 (developing/implementing the AISIA process), Clause 6 (documenting the AISIA) and the informative annexes (incl. Annex A linking to ISO/IEC 42001 clauses 6.1.2/6.1.4/A.5, Annex B linking to ISO/IEC 23894, and the Annex E AISIA template). 3 items are marked CIA-security (impact identification covering security-related harms, integrity of assessment records, confidentiality/access control of records). ISO/IEC 42005 is a guidance document (not a certifiable requirements standard); Clause 5/6 sub-points here are a thematic breakdown of its content, not verbatim numbered subclauses - verify structure and wording against the purchased standard.

Tab 7 - ISO/IEC 27001:2022: 123 items - Clauses 4-10 (30, mandatory ISMS requirements) and Annex A (93 controls). 85 are marked CIA-security. Because ISO/IEC 27001 is itself the information security management standard, most Annex A controls are directly CIA-relevant; the few left unmarked (e.g. 5.1 policies, 5.2 roles, 5.35/5.36 review/compliance, 6.1-6.4 people governance) are administrative/process requirements needed to run the ISMS rather than controls that themselves protect confidentiality, integrity or availability.

Tab 8 - ISO/IEC 17021-1:2015 (requirements for bodies providing audit and certification of management systems): 42 items across Clauses 4-10. The standard governs certification bodies, not certified organizations, so each row gives the CB requirement plus an 'audit-readiness alignment' column showing what your organization should have ready for a certification audit run under it, with cross-references to ISO 27001 / ISO 42001. 11 items are marked CIA-security (confidentiality of client information, integrity of certificates/marks/decisions, protection of audit records). Sector-specific companions apply on top: ISO/IEC 27006-1 (ISMS certification bodies) and ISO/IEC 42006 (AI management system certification bodies) - verify current editions. Subclause numbering follows the 2015 edition; verify against the standard.

Tab 9 - GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679): 39 articles/groups spanning principles, lawful basis, data subject rights, controller/processor obligations, security (Art.32), breach notification (Art.33-34), DPIA (Art.35), DPO (Art.37-39), international transfers and penalties. 13 items are marked CIA-security - the core one is Art.32 (Security of processing), which explicitly requires confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience; Art.33/34 breach notification, Art.24/25 (security-by-design), Art.28 processor contracts and Art.5(1)(f)/9/10/35/46 round out the set. The remaining articles are rights-based, procedural or governance obligations. Requirement text is a condensed paraphrase for compliance planning, not legal advice - verify against the consolidated GDPR text and get qualified legal counsel for interpretation.

Tab 10 - OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (v2.0, published 18 Nov 2024 by the OWASP GenAI Security Project): all 10 risks (LLM01-LLM10), every one CIA-marked - unlike governance frameworks, this list is entirely a security taxonomy, so each risk maps directly to confidentiality, integrity and/or availability impact. Status defaults include 'Accepted risk' since some risks (e.g. LLM09 Misinformation) may be mitigated rather than eliminated. This list applies to LLM/RAG/chatbot applications; if you also run autonomous multi-step agents, the companion OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications adds agent-specific risks (e.g. tool misuse, memory poisoning, cascading failures) on top of this list - ask if you want that added as a further tab. Cross-reference: these risks are the practical, attack-level detail behind ISO 42001 A.6.2.4 (verification/validation), EU AI Act Art.15 (accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity), and NIST AI RMF Measure 2 (secure & resilient testing) in the other tabs.

Tab 11 - ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (PIMS - extension to ISO/IEC 27001/27002 for privacy): 22 items covering Clause 5 (PIMS-specific requirements extending ISO 27001 clauses 4-10), Clause 6 (privacy overlay on the ISO 27002/27001 Annex A control themes), Clause 7 (additional guidance for PII controllers), Clause 8 (additional guidance for PII processors), and Annexes A/B/C-E. 7 items are marked CIA-security - mainly the privacy risk assessment (5.4), technological controls (6.T), and privacy-by-design/minimisation, disposal, sharing/transfer/disclosure and breach-notification items (7.4, 7.5, 8.4, 8.5) that directly protect the confidentiality and integrity of PII. Clause 7/8 and Annex A/B are shown at category level (2019 edition groups ~31 controller and ~18 processor controls under these four categories each); verify individual control wording against the purchased standard, and note ISO/IEC 27701:2025 has since been published as a standalone PIMS standard rather than an ISO 27001 extension. Tab 9 (GDPR) is the closest cross-reference, since Annex D of 27701 maps directly to GDPR articles.

Tab 12 - Master Control List: every item from all 19 framework tabs (557 in total, refreshed to include Tabs 3-11 and 14-22; Tab 19's Data Governance Register is a working template, not a checklist, and is excluded from this count) in one flat, filterable list, grouped by 32 common control domains that cut across frameworks (e.g. Access Control, Risk Assessment, Logging/Monitoring, Incident Management, MITRE ATLAS Tactics, Risk Quantification). Use column A's autofilter to isolate one domain and see every framework's equivalent requirement side by side. Status/Applicable/Owner columns here are for a consolidated, program-level view; the individual framework tabs remain the source of truth for formal audit evidence per standard. This list is rebuilt from the framework tabs as they stood when last refreshed - if you add or edit a framework tab afterward, ask for this tab (and Tab 13) to be refreshed again to stay in sync.

Tab 13 - Domain Crosswalk (Overlap Map): one row per control domain (32 total), showing which frameworks and specific references fall into it, plus consolidation guidance on the control set to implement once so it substantially addresses every framework listed. This answers 'if I fulfil this control, which others does it also address?' - e.g. one secure-SDLC-plus-red-team programme satisfies ISO 27001, ISO 42001 A.6.2.x, EU AI Act Art.15, NIST Measure 2, OWASP LLM Top 10 and ISO/IEC 27090's threat catalogue at once; one incident response plan with tuned notification timelines covers ISO 27001, GDPR Art.33/34, EU AI Act Art.73 and DORA's 4-hour/72-hour/1-month reporting clock together. The last domain, 'Framework-Specific', lists items with no real cross-framework equivalent (e.g. EU AI Act prohibited practices/scope, OECD broad policy recommendations, ISO 17021 certification-body-only clauses) - these must be addressed individually. Refreshed alongside Tab 12; ask for both to be rebuilt again after adding or editing any framework tab.

Domain classification method: each item was matched to a domain by its title/requirement wording using a keyword-based rule set, refined by manual review of edge cases. It is a practical grouping for planning and gap analysis (similar in spirit to a common-controls/crosswalk framework such as the Secure Controls Framework), not an official or certified mapping - a genuine one-to-one equivalence between two standards' wording should still be confirmed against both texts before you rely on it to skip work in an audit.

Tab 14 - Privacy by Design: 20 practical design-checklist items structured around Ann Cavoukian's 7 Foundational Principles of Privacy by Design (Ontario IPC, 2009) - the canonical framework the term originates from, referenced in GDPR Recital 78 and underlying GDPR Art.25 (Tab 9). 9 items are marked CIA-security, concentrated in Principle 5 (End-to-End Security - Full Lifecycle Protection), since that principle is explicitly about applying confidentiality/integrity/availability controls across the data lifecycle; Principle 3's privacy-enhancing technologies and Principle 4's privacy/security synergy are also marked. No single ISO/IEC standard number covers 'privacy by design' end-to-end as a certifiable checklist the way ISO 27001 does for security; the closest formal standards are GDPR Art.25 (legal requirement, Tab 9), ISO/IEC 27701 Clause 7.4/8.4 (Tab 11, PIMS requirements), and ISO/IEC 31700-1:2023 (Consumer protection - Privacy by design for consumer goods and services, a newer ISO standard specifically for consumer products/services) - this tab's items are written to be consistent with all three but are not a verbatim reproduction of any one text.

Tab 15 - ISO/IEC 31700-1:2023 and ISO/IEC TR 31700-2:2023 (Consumer protection - Privacy by design for consumer goods and services): 28 items, structured on Part 1's verified table of contents - Clause 4 General (organizational foundations, 8 sub-clauses), Clause 5 Consumer communication requirements (5), Clause 6 Risk management requirements (5), Clause 7 Developing/deploying/operating privacy controls (8), and Clause 8 End of PII lifecycle requirements (1). Part 2 is a Technical Report of illustrative use cases (not independently certifiable requirements) mapped to Part 1's clauses, shown here as one informative reference row. 14 items are marked CIA-security, concentrated in Clause 6 (privacy risk assessment, and explicitly linking privacy risk to cybersecurity resilience design in 6.6), Clause 7 (designing/implementing/testing/operating privacy controls and managing privacy breaches), and breach-related items in 5.6 and 8.2. Unlike Tab 14 (Cavoukian's 7 principles, a general design philosophy), this is a certifiable ISO standard specifically for consumer-facing goods and services - use Tab 14 for the underlying philosophy and this tab for the ISO-structured, auditable requirement set.

Tab 16 - DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, Digital Operational Resilience Act): 29 items drawn from the operative chapters - Chapter I Scope/Proportionality, Chapter II ICT risk management (Art.5-16), Chapter III incident management/classification/reporting (Art.17-23), Chapter IV resilience testing incl. TLPT (Art.24-27), Chapter V ICT third-party risk incl. Register of Information and CTPP oversight (Art.28-42, summarised), Chapter VI information sharing (Art.45), and a summary of Chapters VII-IX (supervisory powers/penalties, application date). 18 items are marked CIA-security - DORA is a financial-sector operational-resilience regulation, so most of Chapter II (protection, detection, response/recovery, backups) and the testing/incident chapters are directly CIA-relevant, with Art.11/12 and Art.29 specifically tied to availability. Applies to EU-regulated financial entities (see Art.2) and, via Chapter V, to their ICT third-party providers - relevant to Ooredoo's banking/financial-services engagements and any EU-regulated counterparties. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025; numerous Regulatory/Implementing Technical Standards (RTS/ITS) referenced in the articles above add further detail and should be checked for the current version.

Tab 17 - NIST ARIA (Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI): 14 items. IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE FROM OTHER TABS - ARIA is a NIST AI Innovation Lab research TEVV (test, evaluation, validation, verification) PROGRAM, not a certifiable compliance standard with numbered clauses; NIST explicitly states it is not a certification programme. So this tab is a readiness/alignment checklist rather than a requirements checklist: it is organized around ARIA's own three-tier evaluation structure (Model Testing - confirm claimed capabilities; Red Teaming - stress test and attempt to induce risks; Field Testing - examine real-world impacts) plus its composite measurement instrument, the Contextual Robustness Index (CoRIx, ten dimensions including the seven AI RMF trustworthy characteristics - the exact remaining three dimensions beyond those seven were not confirmed from public sources at time of writing and should be checked against NIST's current ARIA Evaluation Design Document). 6 items are marked CIA-security, concentrated in Red Teaming (adversarial testing is explicitly a security-attack simulation) and the 'secure and resilient' CoRIx dimension. ARIA 0.1 currently focuses on LLM applications and is evolving; check https://ai-challenges.nist.gov/aria for the current pilot status, data-handling rules, and whether formal participation is open before committing a system for evaluation. ARIA builds directly on the NIST AI RMF (Tab 5) and the NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile risks, so align this tab's items with Tab 5's Measure function rather than treating ARIA engagement as a separate programme.

Tab 18 - FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) Risk Methodology: 24 items. Built on FAIR as this is the widely-adopted quantitative cyber risk methodology (standardized by the Open Group as Open FAIR O-RA/O-RT, and maintained by the FAIR Institute) - no verified framework named 'FIAR' was found; this tab assumes that was the intended reference. Structured in three parts: the core FAIR taxonomy (Risk, Loss Event Frequency, Threat Event Frequency, Threat Capability, Resistance/Control Strength, Vulnerability, Probable Loss Magnitude and the six forms of loss), the four-stage/ten-step risk assessment process (identify asset and threat community; estimate TEF, TCap and control strength; derive vulnerability and LEF; estimate worst-case and probable loss magnitude; derive and articulate risk, typically via Monte Carlo simulation into a loss exceedance curve), and organizational governance requirements for running FAIR properly (calibrated estimation training, consistent taxonomy, peer review, tooling, integration with the existing risk register, and periodic validation against the Open Group's general requirements for risk assessment methodologies). 13 items are marked CIA-security because FAIR scenarios ultimately quantify the frequency and magnitude of loss from confidentiality, integrity and availability-impacting events - this complements rather than replaces the qualitative risk-assessment clauses already in ISO 27001 (6.1.2/8.2, Tab 7) and ISO 42001 (6.1.2/8.2, Tabs 1-2): use FAIR to add quantified, financial risk expression on top of those existing risk registers for the highest-priority scenarios.

Tab 3 update - a Role Legend (Provider, Deployer, Authorised Representative, Importer, Distributor, Product Manufacturer, Operator umbrella term, GPAI Model Provider - each with its Art.3 definition and key responsibilities) was added at the top of the EU AI Act tab, and a new 'Applicable Role(s) & Responsibilities' column was added to every article row showing which role(s) that specific article binds and what each must do.

Tab 19 - Data Lineage, Provenance & Governance Register: a working template (not a checklist) for cataloguing datasets - especially AI training/operational data - with 16 DAMA-DMBOK-aligned fields (lineage, provenance, source entry, collection method, version information, data licensing, access rights, intended use/purpose limitation, jurisdictional considerations, context, plus data quality notes, ownership and status). A field guide at the top maps each column to the relevant DAMA International Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK) knowledge area - principally Data Governance, Metadata Management, Data Security Management, Data Quality, and Data Architecture - so the rationale for each field is traceable to DAMA guidance rather than invented ad hoc. Two illustrative example rows (generic, not representing real organizational data) show how to complete it, followed by 25 blank rows ready for use. This register operationalizes items already tracked elsewhere in this workbook: ISO 42001 A.7.x data governance (Tabs 1-2), EU AI Act Art.10 data governance (Tab 3), GDPR Records of Processing (Art.30, Tab 9) and cross-border transfer provisions (Art.44-49, Tab 9), and the 'Data Governance, Quality & Provenance' domain in the crosswalk (Tab 13) - use this tab as the detailed, per-dataset evidence that satisfies those higher-level clauses.

Tab 20 - ISO/IEC 5181 (Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Data provenance): 13 items. VERIFIED: title, scope and status were confirmed directly from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27's own listing (iso.org/standard/80971.html) - the standard is real, in final production, expected to publish around October 2026. NOT YET VERIFIED: numbered clause structure - the standard's public text/table of contents is not yet available because it has not been published, so the items in this tab (sections 'T.1'-'T.6' and 'AI.1'-'AI.5') are a topical breakdown inferred from the official scope statement and typical SC27 provenance-standard conventions, not verified clause numbers. Re-check this tab against the published text once ISO/IEC 5181 is formally released, and update references accordingly. 8 items are marked CIA-security, since the standard's own scope is specifically about deriving provenance metadata 'securely' - integrity (tamper-evident, trustworthy provenance records) is the dominant property, with confidentiality relevant to sensitive provenance details and availability relevant to long-term retention. The AI-specific section (AI.1-AI.5) applies the standard's data-asset-provenance techniques to AI training/operational datasets and model lineage, and cross-references ISO 42001 A.7.5 (Tabs 1-2), EU AI Act Art.10 (Tab 3), the Data Governance Register (Tab 19), and OWASP LLM03 Supply Chain (Tab 10). AI.4 also flags that provenance/authenticity of AI-GENERATED content (e.g. deepfake watermarking) is handled by separate content-provenance mechanisms such as C2PA, not by ISO/IEC 5181 itself, which is scoped to data-asset provenance.

Tab 21 - ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (Cybersecurity - Artificial Intelligence - Addressing security threats and compromises to AI systems): 17 items. VERIFIED: this is a genuinely published standard (first edition, October 2026, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27/WG 4), with confirmed structure - Clause 5 Application of information security, Clause 6 Types of potential compromise (the threat catalogue, 12+ scenarios), Clause 7 Mitigations and their interactions, Annex A life-cycle/asset mapping, Annex B AI-specific versions of conventional attacks, Annex C federated machine learning. Clause 6 is itemised here against its named threats (data/model poisoning, evasion, membership inference, model inversion, model stealing, prompt/output injection); 6.8 flags that the full published catalogue has further scenarios beyond these named ones - verify the complete list against the published text. 12 items are marked CIA-security - this is itself purely a security-threat standard, so nearly every item carries a CIA marking; confidentiality dominates the data-extraction threats (membership inference, model inversion, model stealing), integrity dominates the manipulation threats (poisoning, evasion), and prompt/output injection can hit all three depending on what the compromised output feeds into. IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE (from the standard itself): it addresses threats TO an organization's own AI systems, not threats INVOLVING AI used by attackers against others, and explicitly excludes AI-vs-AI attack scenarios. This tab is the natural ISO-governance companion to Tab 10 (OWASP LLM Top 10) - OWASP's list is LLM/GenAI-specific and community-maintained; ISO/IEC 27090 is broader (any AI system, not just LLMs) and integrates into the ISO 27001/42001 management-system structure already used across this workbook. A privacy counterpart, ISO/IEC 27091 (privacy protection for AI), is referenced in industry commentary as a companion standard - ask if you want that added as a further tab.

Tab 22 - MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems): 18 items covering all 16 current ATLAS tactics (Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, AI Model Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, AI Attack Staging, Command and Control, Exfiltration, Impact), verified current as of October 2026. ATLAS mirrors MITRE ATT&CK's structure (tactics as adversary objectives/columns, techniques as methods/rows beneath each, linked to real-world case studies) but is AI/ML-specific; 'AI Model Access' and 'AI Attack Staging' are the two tactics with no direct ATT&CK equivalent and carry the AI-native logic. This tab is deliberately at tactic level (16 rows) rather than enumerating the full ~100+ techniques/sub-techniques, to match the granularity used elsewhere in this workbook - for hands-on red-teaming or detection-engineering work, consult the live matrix at atlas.mitre.org for the current technique list under each tactic, since ATLAS is actively updated (recent releases have added agentic-AI and multi-agent techniques at a fast pace). 15 items are marked CIA-security (Resource Development is the one exception, being purely attacker-side preparation with no direct impact on the target yet). IMPORTANT: ATLAS is a threat-intelligence and red-team/detection reference, not a certifiable compliance checklist like the other standards in this workbook - use it to structure red-team scope and SOC detection use cases, and cross-walk it against your own AI architecture rather than treating every tactic as a control to 'complete'. It complements Tab 10 (OWASP LLM Top 10, which gives the vulnerability-centric view) and Tab 21 (ISO/IEC 27090, which gives the ISO-governance threat view) - ATLAS adds the adversary's full attack-lifecycle perspective with documented real-world case studies behind each technique.

field_guide.description: Unique, stable identifier for the dataset so it can be referenced consistently across systems, risk registers and this workbook's AI/data tabs.
Human-readable name used consistently in catalogues, documentation and conversations about the data.
What business process, product or AI system the data supports, and why it is collected - the context needed to judge whether a use is still within scope.
The authoritative originating system, application, sensor, survey, vendor feed or third party the data first enters the organization from.
How the data was captured - direct entry, API/system integration, web scraping, purchased feed, sensor/IoT, survey, derived/inferred - since method affects quality and consent basis.
The documented chain of custody and transformation from original source to current state, including any third parties the data has passed through.
Where the data flows: upstream systems/datasets it depends on, and downstream systems, reports, models or products that consume it - enabling impact analysis of a change or breach.
Version identifier, extraction/snapshot timestamp, and change history, so a specific state of the data can be reproduced or audited.
The licence or legal basis under which the data may be used (owned, licensed-in with terms, open data licence, public domain) and any restrictions that come with it.
The data's sensitivity classification (e.g. public/internal/confidential/restricted) and who/which roles are authorized to access it, per the organization's access control policy.
The specific, documented purpose(s) the data may be used for - the basis for judging purpose-limitation compliance (e.g. GDPR Art.5(1)(b), Tab 9) and for AI training-data suitability.
Country/region of data residency, applicable data protection law (e.g. GDPR, Qatar PDPPL), and any cross-border transfer mechanism relied upon (see GDPR Tab 9, Art.44-49).
Known quality issues, completeness/accuracy caveats, or quality-assurance checks performed, relevant to anyone using the data (including for AI training per ISO 42001 A.7.4, Tab 2).
The accountable business owner and the operational data steward responsible for maintaining this record and the data's quality/compliance.
Date this register entry was last verified as accurate, supporting periodic review obligations across the frameworks in this workbook.
Current lifecycle status of the dataset entry (e.g. Active, Under review, Deprecated, Scheduled for deletion).
